name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Friday 22 April 1977

clue.text: People are not inclined to believe in this attitude

definitions.text: People are not inclined to believe in this attitude

blocks.clueFragment: People are not inclined to believe in this attitude
blocks.note: surface reading: a belief system that most people reject
setter's reading: the attitude is itself the habit of doubting, so people holding it are by definition not inclined to believe

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an unpopular creed; really the clue describes the doubting frame of mind itself, SCEPTICISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Scepticism is a habitual doubting stance, questioning claims instead of accepting them on trust.

clue.text: A girl once in trouble

indicators.note: being in trouble means being in a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young woman who, in days gone by, got herself into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' looks like a time word, but it is part of the fodder along with 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: Connie is a familiar female first name, short for Constance, so it serves as an example of a girl.

clue.text: Before ten, going to church — ostentation

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Showing off by heading to church before ten o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: CE stands for Church of England, a standard crossword abbreviation for church.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretence can mean a showy display or affectation, a false claim to grandeur, which matches ostentation.

clue.text: Delhi's record ol singular progress?

blocks.note: Delhi is in India, so something of Delhi's is Indian
a file is a record kept on someone

explanation.surface: A query about some record held in Delhi of a single forward march.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ol' is a printing error for 'of' in the original newspaper. 'Singular' plays on single: people walking one behind another.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian file means walking in a single line, one person behind another, a one-at-a-time way of moving forward.

clue.text: On whom (or where) coals of fire may be heaped?

definitions.text: On whom (or where) coals of fire may be heaped?

blocks.note: the biblical phrase heaping coals of fire on someone's head means repaying ingratitude or wrong with kindness, so the person is an ungrateful one
split differently, the word also names the place coals of fire sit: inside a fireplace's iron basket

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb from Romans 12:20 says kindness to an enemy heaps coals of fire on his head; read as two words the answer becomes IN GRATE, where real coals go.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, the kind on whom one heaps coals of fire by returning good for evil.

clue.text: Run in a heat, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: competing in a qualifying race at an athletics meeting
setter's reading: what wax or butter does when it gets hot, running as liquid

explanation.walkthrough: A heat is a preliminary race, but here it is literal warmth that makes something run.
explanation.definitionFit: To melt is to turn liquid under warmth, so a solid that melts runs in heat.

clue.text: Cut-out action when noise rises around 91

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading from the bottom upwards, so the word runs backwards
around means wrapping one piece about another, enclosing it

blocks.note: taken as written
91 in Roman numerals is XC (90) plus I (1)

explanation.surface: A cutting-out operation timed for when the racket swells around number 91.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rises' reads upwards, and the Roman numeral sits inside after the first letter rather than at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Excision is the act of cutting something out, as in surgery or editing, so it is a cut-out action.

clue.text: 14's spirit to dance? That's for suckers!

blocks.note: the spirit in the answer to 14 down is brandy
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: An invitation to dance on 14's spirits, dismissed as only for fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suckers' looks like an insult for dupes, but means people who suck sweets. A brandy-ball is a British boiled sweet flavoured with brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy-ball is a hard boiled sweet meant to be sucked slowly, so it is made for those who suck.

clue.text: Methuselah's tipple?

blocks.note: Methuselah lived 969 years in Genesis, the longest life in the Bible
his favourite drink would be the legendary potion granting long life

explanation.walkthrough: The joke imagines Methuselah's great age came from drinking the elixir of life.
explanation.definitionFit: An elixir is a magical potion, especially the alchemists' draught believed to prolong life indefinitely.

clue.text: A low cur often has our sympathy

definitions.text: A low cur often has our sympathy

blocks.note: under means beneath, low down
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: A mongrel kept down by others tends to win our pity.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer while 'low cur' builds it: the dog at the bottom is the one we root for.
explanation.definitionFit: An underdog is the competitor expected to lose, and onlookers traditionally side with such a weaker party.

clue.text: Revolutionary clubman?

blocks.note: surface reading: a political radical; setter's reading: to do with turning wheels, rotation
a member of a club, here the service organisation named after a wheel

explanation.walkthrough: Rotary International, a businessmen's service club, takes its name and wheel emblem from rotation, so its member is 'revolutionary'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Rotarian is a member of a Rotary Club, a service organisation whose name comes from rotating meeting places.

clue.text: Tacked in all directions

blocks.note: the four compass points south, east, west and north

explanation.surface: Sailing by tacking, zigzagging every which way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tacked' suggests a sailing boat changing course, fitting 'all directions', but here it means stitched.
explanation.definitionFit: To tack is to stitch loosely with long temporary stitches, so something tacked has been sewn.

clue.text: Most concrete of virtues

blocks.note: surface reading: the most tangible, practical of good qualities
setter's reading: concrete is solid, and the virtue in question begins with that word

explanation.walkthrough: The answer starts with SOLID, so it is literally the most concrete-sounding virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Solidarity is unity and mutual support within a group, a valued quality of standing together.

clue.text: It isn't cleverness, apparently that makes a person distinguished

blocks.note: isn't contains the negative not
ability is talent or cleverness

explanation.surface: It is not intelligence that sets a person apart from others.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, NOT ABILITY, and the clue seems to deny what the whole word means.
explanation.definitionFit: Notability is the quality of being notable or eminent, the standing that marks someone out.

clue.text: Spirit photograph? It takes the biscuit!

blocks.note: brandy is a distilled spirit
a snap is a casual photograph

explanation.surface: A photo of a ghost is beyond belief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit photograph' suggests ghost pictures; 'takes the biscuit' is a British idiom for being outrageous, but here the answer literally is the biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy-snap is a thin, crisp rolled ginger biscuit, so it really does count as a biscuit.

clue.text: A blooming underhand attack by an essayist

blocks.note: a lob is a ball delivered underarm, as in cricket lob bowling
Elia was the pen-name of the essayist Charles Lamb

explanation.surface: A sly blasted assault from a writer of essays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like a mild British swear word qualifying the attack, but it means flowering. 'Underhand' means underarm, not sneaky.
explanation.definitionFit: Lobelia is a garden plant grown for its small blue flowers, so it is something that blooms.

clue.text: The rotters are for the high jump

blocks.note: first meaning: cads, ill-mannered men, in old British slang
second meaning: those who leap, as athletes entered in a jumping event

explanation.walkthrough: 'For the high jump' is also a British idiom meaning about to be punished, which suits rotters in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A bounder is a dishonourable man in dated slang, and literally one who bounds or leaps upward.

clue.text: Get a man to change colour

indicators.note: changing the preceding words means altering their order into a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Persuade a fellow to switch hue, or perhaps to blush.
explanation.definitionFit: Magenta is a purplish-red shade, a hue named after a battle of 1859.

clue.text: Joined forces

blocks.note: surface reading: teamed up, combined efforts with others
setter's reading: signed up for the armed services

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for cooperating hides its literal sense of becoming a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enlisted is to have signed up for military service, literally joining the armed forces.

clue.text: Islander who could make it copyright

blocks.note: a native of a Mediterranean island
the islander's letters rearranged spell copyright as it sounds, with the silent gh left out

explanation.walkthrough: COPYRIGHT is pronounced copy-rite, and those seven sounded letters are exactly the letters of CYPRIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cypriot is a native or inhabitant of Cyprus, an island in the eastern Mediterranean.

clue.text: Rendered black and blue, this villain?

definitions.text: Rendered black and blue, this villain?

blocks.note: surface reading: beaten up; setter's reading: coloured twice, once black and once blue
the phrase is a stock description of an utter, thoroughgoing scoundrel

explanation.walkthrough: A thoroughgoing villain is called a double-dyed villain; two colours applied make him literally dyed twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Double-dyed means thoroughgoing or out-and-out, used of incorrigible rogues, from cloth dyed twice for fast colour.

clue.text: Faithful in trouble always

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the following words, spanning the gap between them

blocks.note: the end of trouble runs into the start of always

explanation.definitionFit: Leal is a Scottish and literary word for loyal or true, as in 'the land o' the leal'.

clue.text: She starts the day divinely

blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who begins her morning beautifully
setter's reading: a goddess, whose role is to bring the dawn

explanation.walkthrough: 'Divinely' sounds like a compliment but marks her as a deity.
explanation.definitionFit: Aurora is the Roman goddess of the dawn, who opens each morning by bringing light.

clue.text: Motorist's contribution to a house-warming?

blocks.note: a part every car has, which keeps the engine cool
surface reading: a party for a new home; setter's reading: literally heating a house

explanation.walkthrough: The same word names a car's cooling part and a household heater, so the motorist brings one to warm the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A radiator is both the car's engine-cooling unit and a panel heater warming the rooms of a home.

clue.text: Thanks again — goodbye

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thank you
the same word repeated a second time

explanation.surface: Thanking someone twice as you take your leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Ta-ta is a casual British way of saying farewell, an informal parting word.

clue.text: This key to open roads

blocks.note: surface reading: a means of access; setter's reading: the key a driver turns to start a car
once the engine fires, the open road is available to the driver

explanation.walkthrough: Key suggests the secret to freedom, but it is the actual car key that starts the motor.
explanation.definitionFit: The ignition is the system that fires a car engine, switched on by a key, so without it no journey starts.

clue.text: The rat can be a real menace

indicators.note: can be suggests the words may become something else when rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rat is a genuine danger to people and their homes.
explanation.definitionFit: A threat is a source of danger or an intimidating warning, something that genuinely menaces.

clue.text: One diametrically opposed to us?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who completely disagrees with us
setter's reading: someone living at the far end of the Earth's diameter from where we stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Diametrically' is literal: the other end of a line through the Earth's centre. From Britain the antipodes are Australia and New Zealand; in a Canberra paper the joke turns around.
explanation.definitionFit: An antipodean is a person from the opposite side of the globe, especially Australasia as seen from Britain.
